note: Areas are approximate (a few kilometres). The war continues: this storyboard ends at 31 December 2024.

chapters.title: Crimea and Donbas, 2014–2015
arrows: Russian and separatist forces advance to the Azov coast
Separatist and Russian forces take Debaltseve
chapters.text: On 27 February 2014, days after protests in Kyiv ousted President Yanukovych, Russian special forces without insignia began seizing Crimea, which Russia annexed on 18 March; Ukraine and most countries do not recognise the annexation. In April armed pro-Russian groups seized towns in Donbas, including Sloviansk, which Ukrainian forces retook in July. From late August Russian regular troops joined the fighting, encircling Ukrainian units at Ilovaisk and pushing to the Azov coast at Novoazovsk; after the Minsk agreements and the fall of Debaltseve in February 2015 the line barely moved until 2022. Areas for 2014 are approximate.

chapters.title: The invasion and the drive on Kyiv
arrows: Russian advance from Belarus towards Kyiv
Russian advance from the north-east towards Kyiv
chapters.text: On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion. In the north its forces drove from Belarus past Chernobyl towards Kyiv, landed airborne troops at the Antonov airport in Hostomel and took Bucha and Irpin's outskirts, while other columns besieged Chernihiv and pushed from the Sumy region towards Kyiv's eastern suburbs. Kyiv, Chernihiv and Sumy held out. The map shows the areas Russian forces were reported to control, which in the north were often only roads and the villages along them.

chapters.title: Russia withdraws from the north
arrows: Ukrainian forces retake Irpin, Bucha and Hostomel
chapters.text: At the end of March Russia announced it would scale back around Kyiv and Chernihiv and pulled its forces out of the north. Ukrainian troops entered Bucha on 1 April, and the next day the whole Kyiv region was declared retaken; the siege of Chernihiv ended on 4 April. In Bucha and nearby towns the retreating forces left behind the bodies of hundreds of civilians, evidence of killings now investigated as war crimes.

chapters.title: The land bridge and Mariupol
arrows: Russian advance from Crimea to Kherson
Russian advance to Melitopol and Berdiansk
chapters.text: From Crimea, Russian forces advanced quickly across the south: Melitopol was taken on 25–26 February and Kherson, the only regional capital Russia captured in 2022, on 1–2 March, while other columns reached Enerhodar and its nuclear power plant. Mariupol was surrounded and besieged; on 16 March an air strike destroyed its drama theatre, where civilians were sheltering. The last defenders in the Azovstal steelworks surrendered on 20 May, completing a land corridor from Russia to Crimea.

chapters.title: The battle for Donbas and the Kharkiv counteroffensive
arrows: Russian offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk
chapters.text: Russia then concentrated on Donbas, advancing slowly with heavy artillery; it took Sievierodonetsk on 25 June and Lysychansk on 3 July, completing its capture of Luhansk region. In early September Ukraine struck in Kharkiv region: from Balakliia its forces broke through to Kupiansk and Izium by 10–11 September, and on 1 October they retook Lyman. In about a month Ukraine regained most of Kharkiv region.

chapters.title: Kherson retaken
arrows: Ukrainian advance on Kherson from Mykolaiv
chapters.text: On 29 August Ukraine began a counteroffensive on the west bank of the Dnipro, striking the bridges that supplied Russian troops there. After weeks of slow fighting it broke through in the north in early October. On 9 November Russia ordered a withdrawal across the river, and Ukrainian troops entered Kherson on 11 November. Russia had proclaimed the annexation of the Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk regions on 30 September, a move almost all countries reject.

chapters.title: Bakhmut and the 2023 counteroffensive
chapters.text: After nearly ten months of fighting, Russian forces, many from the Wagner Group, captured Bakhmut on 20 May 2023. In June Ukraine launched its long-planned counteroffensive in Zaporizhzhia region, but minefields and fortified lines held it to small gains: it retook a string of villages, including Staromaiorske in July and Robotyne in August, and some ground around Bakhmut. The front barely moved by the end of the year.

chapters.title: Avdiivka, the push on Pokrovsk and the Kursk incursion
chapters.text: Russia took Avdiivka on 17 February 2024 after a four-month battle and kept advancing west towards Pokrovsk, taking Selydove in October; in May it also opened a new front north of Kharkiv around Vovchansk. On 6 August Ukraine sent troops across the border into Russia's Kursk region, taking the town of Sudzha; Russia, later joined by North Korean troops, slowly pushed them back. The war was still going on when the map data ends at the close of 2024.

battles.casualties: 267 Ukrainian soldiers killed; separatist and Russian losses disputed (58–868)

battles.casualties: disputed: 200 Ukrainian (Russian claim) to 300–500 Russian (Ukrainian claim) killed

battles.casualties: 700+ civilians killed; several hundred soldiers on each side (claims)

battles.name: Kherson counteroffensive
